summary: The run accumulated avoidable HP losses before reaching the final fight: it paid 16 HP for random upgrades, chose smithing while at 57/80 HP, and later accepted a curse despite already being under pressure. HP then fell from 57 to 43, 30, 18, and finally 5, leaving little margin for the last combat. The final combat also showed questionable low-HP sequencing, with two Defends and an Ancient Potion used while both enemies remained alive.

lessons.title: Choose recovery when the HP trajectory is deteriorating
lessons.situation: At a campfire when current HP is already substantially below maximum and several combats remain before the boss.
lessons.lesson: Prefer resting over smithing when the run has already incurred meaningful damage and there is no clear evidence that the upgrade is necessary for an imminent fight. Preserving enough HP to survive multiple future combats is more valuable than a marginal early upgrade.
evidence_points: At Act 1 Floor 6, HP was 57/80 and the alternatives were rest, smith, and recall; smith was chosen.
After that decision, HP fell to 43 on Floor 8, 30 on Floor 10, 18 on Floor 11, and 5 on Floor 12.
lessons.reasoning: The subsequent sequence shows that the run lacked enough HP buffer for the remaining path. Resting at Floor 6 would not guarantee survival, but it would directly address the demonstrated resource problem, whereas the chosen smith did not prevent continued HP loss.

lessons.title: Do not take a curse-for-gold deal while already under HP pressure
lessons.situation: When an event offers substantial gold in exchange for a permanent curse and the run is already damaged or lacks a concrete plan to spend the gold.
lessons.lesson: Favor the safer event option unless the gold is immediately needed for a high-impact purchase. A permanent curse adds deck dilution and future draw risk while the extra gold may not improve survival.
evidence_points: At Act 1 Floor 7, HP was 57/80 and the run chose to gain 175 gold and become cursed with Doubt.
Doubt remained in the final 20-card deck, while the trajectory shows no later shop purchase after this event.
lessons.reasoning: The decision traded survivability and deck quality for gold that was not shown to produce a later benefit. This is especially costly in a run already taking repeated combat damage.

lessons.title: At critical HP, avoid spending the turn without a concrete threat-reduction plan
lessons.situation: When starting a combat at very low HP and the opening hand contains both attacks and defensive cards, especially when potions are available.
lessons.lesson: Sequence actions around immediate survival or rapid removal of a threat. Do not automatically spend most of the opening energy on repeated Defends and then use a potion late in the turn if the logged state shows no immediate additional block or damage benefit.
evidence_points: The final combat began at 5/80 HP with Bash, two Strikes, two Defends, and 3 energy; the first action was Defend.
A second Defend was played, leaving 1 energy and 10 block, then Ancient Potion was used; the state still showed 10 block and both enemies alive before a single Strike was played.
At the start of Turn 2, the player had 5 HP and 0 block while Spike Slime and Looter were both still alive.
lessons.reasoning: The logged sequence does not prove which alternative would have won, because exact damage values are unavailable, but it does show that the chosen line consumed most of the turn without eliminating either threat and failed to preserve block into the next turn. At 5 HP, potion timing and attack-versus-block sequencing should be evaluated for immediate impact rather than played passively.
